paras: The whipping of Ned Sparkman was an attack by a crowd of masked men on a Black preacher at his house near Bethune, South Carolina, in late June 1903. The attackers whipped him, fired into his house, wounding him in the face, and ordered him to leave the community. The papers disagreed on whether the attackers were white or Black.

Sparkman was a local preacher who lived about five miles below Bethune. The Bethune correspondent described him as a man of "rather unsavory reputation" and wrote that "it seems" he had been "talking too much about some parties in the neighborhood."

According to a dispatch dated Bethune, June 23, the crowd came to his house on the previous Saturday night. After giving him a severe whipping, the men fired several shots into the house, and one struck Sparkman in the face, causing what the dispatch called "a painful though not a dangerous wound." They then told him to leave the community at once.
When the dispatch was written, Sparkman had not left. No report of an arrest or investigation appears in the coverage.

The attack drew brief notice in three South Carolina white weeklies. The Batesburg Advocate ran it first, on June 24, as a single unnamed line among its "Late News" items, stating that "White caps whipped a colored preacher" and "then shot him." The Lancaster Ledger printed the fuller Bethune dispatch on June 27 as "Warmed Up the Preacher," giving his reputation and talk as the apparent cause without condemning the crowd. The Newberry Herald and News condensed the same story into its state-news column.
No Black-press coverage of the attack was found.

The Bethune dispatch placed the attack on Saturday night, June 20, while the Batesburg item of June 24 said it happened "last night" and the Newberry paper said "last week"; the datelined local report is the more specific. The papers also differed on the attackers: the Batesburg Advocate called them "White caps," while the Bethune correspondent wrote that "the crowd was supposed to have been negroes."

bases: A night crowd of masked men, called 'white caps' by one paper, whipped a Black preacher at his home, fired into the house and ordered him to leave the community (A1, A3).
The Batesburg brief (A1) and the Bethune dispatch (A3, condensed in A2) agree that a Black preacher near Bethune was whipped and shot, though they differ on the date and on who the attackers were.

framing.detail: The Batesburg Advocate gave the attack one line among 'Late News' items, naming the attackers 'White caps'.

The Lancaster Ledger headed the dispatch 'Warmed Up the Preacher', called Sparkman of 'rather unsavory reputation' and offered his talk about neighbors as the apparent reason, without condemning the attack.
The Newberry Herald and News condensed the dispatch into a state-news roundup, keeping the 'unsavory reputation' wording.
